issues.item: Triggers: Sexual Trauma Cues: Comments on sexual violence
issues.explanation: For a male torture survivor, sexual-trauma-specific verbal cues are possible only if sexual torture or sexual humiliation is part of the trauma, but the rest of the profile provides no corresponding sexual content in memory, appraisals, threat, or coping. As selected, this trigger appears disconnected from the trauma representation and is hard to justify clinically.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The appraisal that others can visibly see what happened to him implies shame/marked visible contamination or exposure. That could occur after torture, but here it is not supported by the memory items, trigger content, or other appraisals, making it feel mismatched with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Gambling: I gamble to distract myself or feel excitement
issues.explanation: Gambling as a coping strategy is not impossible, but in this profile it is poorly linked to the active formulation. The main connected pattern is triggers ↔ negative appraisals with memory-linked re-experiencing and threat-driven compliance/detachment. Gambling introduces a separate excitement-seeking coping style that is not reflected elsewhere and feels clinically disconnected rather than integrated.

vignette:
Rodrigo is a seventy-year-old widowed Salvadoran man who has worked as a welder for most of his adult life. He was referred for psychological evaluation following a significant deterioration in his functioning over the past year, and he presents with a PCL-5 score of 80, consistent with severe post-traumatic stress disorder. The events that brought him to this point reach back decades, but their hold on him has never loosened.

Approximately thirty years ago, Rodrigo was detained by paramilitaries during a period of political violence in his home country. He was held in a windowless room - a concrete cell with no visible exit, no way to call for help, and no indication of when or whether he would be released. Over several days, he was subjected to repeated acts of physical violence. At one point, a guard discharged a firearm inside the building - not at him, but close enough that the concussive sound filled the room entirely. That sound, the absolute absence of options, and the reality of violence as something that could be done to a human body without consequence: these became the architecture of his terror. He survived. He emigrated. He built a life, married, worked with his hands, and for years told himself it was behind him. His wife died three years ago, and the structure that had helped him contain his past collapsed with her.

Rodrigo now works in a fabrication shop, and it is there that the present intrudes most forcefully on the past. The sharp crack of metal striking metal, the occasional pneumatic discharge of equipment nearby - any sudden percussive sound at the shop floor can stop him mid-weld, his body flooding with certainty that the noise is a gunshot. In those moments the memory does not feel like something that happened thirty years ago; it feels like it is happening now, the cell walls present, the air close. When these sensory triggers arrive, Rodrigo finds himself detaching from the memory almost involuntarily, pulling back from it as though from a flame, and simultaneously working hard to suppress whatever images are surfacing. He has described trying to "push it back down" as a near-constant mental effort during his shifts. Situations that feel constraining - being asked to stay late when he hadn't planned on it, finding himself in a small equipment closet, or simply being told what to do in a tone that carries any edge of authority - carry the same charge as the cell did, and these moments of felt entrapment reliably pull the memory forward into the present, vivid and unfinished.

What makes these intrusions so destabilising is not only their sensory intensity but the appraisals that arrive with them. Rodrigo has come to believe, with a conviction that feels like fact, that you can never truly know who will harm you - that violence is latent in ordinary people and ordinary situations, and that his failure to detect it before his detention is evidence of a permanent blindness in himself. This belief that threat is everywhere and unknowable keeps him hypervigilant in ways that make the triggers more likely to fire: a stranger's raised voice, a coworker moving quickly behind him, any scene of physical conflict on television - all of these are scanned for the signature of what happened in that room. His appraisals and his triggers feed one another in a loop he cannot see clearly enough to interrupt. Worse, he carries a crushing conviction that he bears responsibility for what was done to him - that he acted in ways that brought it on - and that he failed to stop it when he should have. When the memory surfaces and he feels the rage that accompanies recall, that rage turns inward almost immediately, folding into guilt and self-recrimination. In those states, he becomes outwardly deferential, almost placatory, agreeing with whatever is asked of him - a fawn response he does not fully understand but which feels, in the moment, like the only safe posture.

When he tries to explain any of this to his adult children, he loses the thread. The account fragments; he cannot finish sentences. He has stopped trying. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment at work when a younger colleague accidentally dropped a steel plate and Rodrigo, without fully understanding what he was doing, pressed himself against the wall and could not move for several minutes. He is most afraid that what happened to him has permanently changed who he is. What he hopes, quietly and with some embarrassment, is that someone might help him find a way to live in the present tense again.
